# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

screens.why4: One row, one gain, eight words, not overlapping anything, and it's the one I lead with; I have nothing to add or cut.
screens.why5: It still means what I typed, following more without asking anyone to repeat, and the hard case 'the last time they lost the conversation with hearing people' is my problem in my words.
screens.why7: There's one benefit, at most 9 words, naming what changes against today's nodding along, and the belief carries it on the hurt case, not any last conversation; the bar is set by Keel at no more than 1 in 3 no difference or worse, so it can hold or fail.
screens.instead: Row: 'Following more of the talk without asking for repeats'; belief: '...would have let them follow more of the talk without asking for repeats.'

screens.why1: After saying how it fits and what it does better, asking what the wearer must take on to start is the obvious next question, and it is the last of the four solution screens.
screens.why2: "What will they have to do to start using it?" with a hint naming setup, extra steps or learning is plain on first read, and I answered it in my own words at once.
screens.why3: I know exactly what a wearer has to do (put the glasses on in the conversation, keep them charged), because it is my product and my users' days.
screens.why4: There is a free box with a 1-to-4, 9-word limit and the *I'm not sure* chip, which correctly lets me leave the dimension out, and nothing is missing or odd.
screens.why5: The screen only takes my words, and what I typed ("Wear the caption glasses in conversations; Charge the glasses every day") sits there unchanged.
screens.why7: The box asks for the effort the wearer takes themselves (setup, steps, learning, which leaves room for the new habit), within the card's 1 to 4 and 9 words, with the founder-side escape the card allows; both my rows are the wearer's own steps and repeat neither Compatibility nor Purchase friction.

screens.why1: Right after I said what they'll have to do to start, it makes sense to check how Keel wrote those efforts down before I pick one to test.
screens.why2: Both rows are plain to me and to my wearers, though the intro opens by repeating its own title, 'What they'll have to do', which reads like a glitch.
screens.why3: Wearing the glasses in a conversation and charging them are things my wearers do themselves and know from their own week.
screens.why4: The two rows are distinct efforts in my wearers' own terms, neither nonsense nor overlapping, and no row is missing that belongs on this screen.
screens.why5: The first row keeps my effort (wearing the glasses, with the phone pairing rightly left to Compatibility), but 'Charge the glasses every day' is not mine and is shown as an ordinary row rather than as Keel's addition.
screens.why7: Both rows are steps the wearer takes and pass the measure, but the second is Keel's daily-habit suggestion sitting inside the list with no why and no marking, where the card wants it last, apart from the 1 to 4, with its reason.
screens.instead: Keep 'Wear the caption glasses in conversations' as my row, and show 'Charge the glasses every day' below it marked as Keel's suggestion, with its why: it is the new daily habit that first use asks.

screens.why1: Right after I checked the effort rows, picking which one strangers will be asked about is the obvious next step in testing my solution.
screens.why2: 'Wear the caption glasses in conversations' and 'Charge the glasses every day' are exactly how I and my users talk about AirCaps, so I can pick on first reading.
screens.why3: I know from power users and returns which habits stick, so I can say which effort is most likely to stop a deaf or hard-of-hearing adult.
screens.why4: The two rows are distinct real efforts: putting visible glasses on in front of hearing people versus a daily charging habit, with no overlap and nothing silly.
screens.why5: My row 'Wear the caption glasses in conversations' is served word for word, and the belief restates it without drift.
screens.why7: Both rows are steps the wearer takes themselves, each one effort in base-form verbs in the third-person voice, with no sign-off, no Compatibility or Purchase-friction overlap and the new habit of use present; the picked belief can be supported or refuted against the 1-in-3 bar.

screens.why1: After the solution beliefs and before people see the study, asking whether to collect emails from people who would try the caption glasses is the natural closing step for a founder with a commitment step in mind.
screens.why2: Pilot, email and a yes/no are plain to me as a founder, and the hint shows the exact line respondents will see.
screens.why3: Whether I want leads for people who'd order the glasses is my own call, answered from what I'm doing this week.
screens.why4: Yes or no is complete and distinct for an on/off choice, and no escape is needed for the founder's own decision.
screens.why5: My commitment step was 'order the caption glasses with free returns', but the respondent line says only 'try this for real', so the free-returns order I typed is not what strangers are asked and the screen does not show it.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes see: "Would you order the caption glasses with free returns? Leave your email." -- Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Picking who interviews my respondents belongs here, right before the study goes out, after the pilot offer.
screens.why2: The question and hint are plain to me: a voice, a 5-second sample, a cost, and the link by text.
screens.why3: I can pick a voice, but my respondents are deaf and hard-of-hearing, so the voice matters little to many of them and I'd be guessing which suits them; what I really need to know is that the written questions and captions come first.
screens.why4: Daphne and Saskia are distinct and the hint says people can read and type, but there is no text-only or captions-first choice, which is the one many of my deaf respondents would pick; the hint also says 'voice' where my recorded answer says 'face'.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or roles leaks onto this screen, and it only frames how my own questions are delivered.
screens.instead: Who should ask deaf or hard-of-hearing adults your questions? Every question is written on screen with live captions, and people can type or tap. Daphne (voice + captions) / Saskia (voice + captions) / Text only, no voice

screens.why1: Choosing how strangers will answer belongs right after choosing who asks the questions and just before sending, so it sits where I expect it.
screens.why2: The three choices are short and plain, and saying every question is also written on the screen answers my first worry for deaf and hard-of-hearing respondents.
screens.why3: I know my wearers rely on text and captions, so I can pick from what I know of them without guessing.
screens.why4: The options are distinct and complete, but Read and tap offers to let them speak into a box, which may not suit Deaf respondents who do not speak.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product leaks into the options, and the screen keeps my actor's words, deaf or hard-of-hearing adults.
screens.instead: How should deaf or hard-of-hearing adults answer? Read and tap (type or tap every answer) / AI interviewer Daphne, every question also captioned on screen / Let them choose

screens.why1: This is the last step before sending, right after choosing how people answer, so it is clear why Keel asks who gets a link.
screens.why2: The choices are clear, but the second one switches from 'I' to 'you' and names a 'Contacts page' I have not seen yet in this flow, so it takes a second read.
screens.why3: I know whether I am reaching deaf and hard-of-hearing people I know by name, like users from the TranscribeGlass days, or posting in a group where they already gather.
screens.why4: The three ways are distinct and cover my real routes: people I know, a Keel search, and one link posted in an HLAA chapter or Deaf community group.
screens.why5: Nothing here changes my study or leaks AirCaps or the wearer role; it is only about delivery.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? -- People I know by name (I send each their own link) / People I find with a Keel search (Keel makes a link for each; I send them) / A group where they already are (I post one open link; each person signs in with Google)

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits under the title, and the tally (3 beliefs: 3 holding) plus each card's "7 of 7 · bar 5 of 7" show the numbers behind it, tied by "the verdict is the worst of all its cards".
screens.why_b2: Each card says what was counted (said yes / would have gone better / would do it), over how many (of 7), and where the bar sits (5 of 7), all on first look.
screens.why_b3: The dimension names and the three belief lines are recognisably mine, but the solution statement under the title is garbled: it says "the app on the lightweight glasses shows live captions" and then "gets back live captions" twice, which is not how I would describe AirCaps.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the page says what three holding beliefs mean for AirCaps or what I should do next; the only explanatory line describes how the verdict is computed.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and the 3 conditional wearers are flagged, but calling every belief "Holding up" off 7 people never mentions that 7 is a small sample.
screens.instead: Holding up on 7 people, a small sample: all 7 could read captions while watching faces and would wear the glasses, though 3 only on a condition; check what those conditions were before you price, and say the solution in one clean line: captions of the people nearby, shown inside the lens of glasses paired to your phone.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 7 of 7 said yes against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: Four bars with for/against marked, a strip of 7 cells all for, and the marker at 5 make the count, the n and the bar plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility and 'could read captions while watching faces' are the row I picked; only the bar line's clipped 'You said could read...' reads a little odd.
screens.why_b4: The So line tells me this condition isn't my risk and points me to Adoption friction as the one to work on, which is a concrete next look.
screens.why_b5: The count line honestly says a small group is a lean, not a call, but the So line then states flatly that this 'is not what will stop them' on seven people, and I'd also want to know that a unanimous yes may mean my segment already settles this.
screens.instead: With all 7 saying yes, reading captions while watching faces looks unlikely to be what stops them, though 7 is a small group and a unanimous yes may mean most of your segment already does this; Adoption friction, below, is the open question.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 7 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and which number decided it.
screens.why_b2: The strip makes the count, the n and the bar plain, but the chart's 'Better · 7 7 a lot · 0 a little' doubles the 7 and shows no 'No difference' or 'Worse' at zero, so I had to read it twice.
screens.why_b3: The dimension's name, the hard case (losing the conversation with hearing people) and my benefit 'more of the talk followed without asking for repeats' are the words I checked.
screens.why_b4: It says the imagined advantage is in and sends me to Adoption friction, whether they would actually wear the caption glasses, which is the real open question for me.
screens.why_b5: It is honest about the small group and the hypothetical, but the question called AirCaps 'an app' when it is caption glasses, and the card does not flag that seven people rated a phone app, not what I sell.
screens.instead: Ask and show it as 'AirCaps, caption glasses paired to your phone', and draw all four answers in the chart with No difference and Worse at 0, so 7 of 7 better is read against what could have refuted it.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 7 of 7 would do it against a bar of 5 of 7, and the 3 conditional yeses are split out, so I know the belief held and by what margin.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four fixed answers over the 7 people who answered, the strip shows 7 cells for me with the marker at 5, and the 1-in-3 rule is spelled out under it, all plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: Adoption friction and 'Most would wear the caption glasses in conversations' are my row as I picked it; the stranger's 'the glasses' is the same step.
screens.why_b4: The So line points me to the notes below for what would make it worth it, but every condition is comfort through a conversation, and none of the notes speak to it. Harriet wants a trial under stage lights, Ruth wants audience questions picked up, and Tomás's seat trick works, so I am left without a concrete step such as all-day comfort or a try-before-you-order loan.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 stays visible and 'a lean, not a call' is said, but 'what would make it worth it to those 3 is below' claims the quotes answer the comfort condition when none of them do.
screens.instead: 4 of 7 would wear them as is, 3 only if they stay comfortable through a whole conversation; comfort, not willingness, is the catch, so lead with weight and wear time and a no-risk first try (one of the 3 asked to borrow a pair first).

screens.why_b1: The status word 'Holding up' sits right beside '7 of 7 would do it · bar 5 of 7', so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b3: 'Adoption friction' and 'Most would wear the caption glasses in conversations' are the dimension and the belief line as I checked them, after the revision-24 rewording.
screens.why_b4: The only framing is 'Adoption friction held, 7 of 7; what they added:'. Nothing turns Harriet's borrow-first ask or Ruth's audience-pickup ask into a concrete move like a loaner or demo pair, or far-field mic testing.
screens.why_b5: Every quote carries the same truncated label 'Only if it stays comfortable through a conversation for', but Harriet's condition is reading the lens under stage lights, Ruth's is catching audience questions, and Tomás describes a workaround that already works, so the screen misstates what the 3 conditional yeses hinged on while still headlining 7 of 7.
screens.why_b6: I did not type any of these: try-before-buy at one matinee, lens legibility under stage lighting, the mics missing audience questions in a big hall, and a one-sided-deaf user whose seat trick makes the glasses less needed.

screens.why1: As the first screen it is obvious why they ask: they want to know whether I deal with hearing people often enough to be part of this, and I can see that straight away.
screens.why2: "Hearing people" is how we say it in the deaf community, so I understand it on first read without stopping.
screens.why3: I know exactly how often I talk with hearing people, at work, at the shops and with family, so I can answer from my own week.
screens.why4: Yes or no is complete for a gate like this, and having no escape is right for a screener.
screens.why5: It asks only who I talk with, in the words of the founder's segment, and nothing about a product or plan reaches me here.
screens.why6: It is short and one question, and two options are easy to hold; "I'll read 2 options" is a little stiff next to the plain "Yes or no" the guidelines give a screener, but it still says well.
screens.instead: Do you talk face to face with hearing people every week? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after I said I talk with hearing people every week, it makes sense to ask whether one of those talks went wrong for me this week.
screens.why2: 'Lose track of a conversation' is exactly how I'd put it: the moment I've lost the thread and I'm nodding along.
screens.why3: I know straight away whether that happened to me in the last seven days; I don't have to guess.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it, and the chips only show with the story box after a Yes, so they don't muddle the gate.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product, an app or captions slips in; it only asks about my week.
screens.why6: It's one short sentence with 'Yes or no' at the end, easy to take in once, whether I'm reading the captions or lipreading.
screens.why7: Two fixed answers, Yes then No, with no escape; the stem names the window and the thing that goes wrong, not just talking with hearing people, so someone whose week was all easy one-to-ones can honestly say No.

screens.why1: After two questions about losing track of conversations with hearing people, showing me the idea is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Live captions, glasses and eye contact are all words I use every day as someone who relies on captions.
screens.why3: It's about the conversations I have face to face, so I can picture it straight away.
screens.why4: A card to read, no options.
screens.why5: It's shown on purpose as an idea, and the belief about keeping eye contact reads like the founder's own aim without slipping in any odd terms.
screens.why6: Heard once, the second line just repeats the first (lightweight glasses, the app, live captions inside the lens), so it drags before getting to the point about eye contact.
screens.instead: Imagine AirCaps, an app on lightweight glasses that shows live captions inside the lens. When people near you talk, you read their words in the lens as they speak. The people building it believe it would let you read the words while keeping eye contact.

screens.why1: Right after the AirCaps card, asking whether I could read captions and still watch faces is the obvious first worry for someone like me who lip-reads.
screens.why2: Reading captions while watching faces is exactly how I would say it; no word is strange to me.
screens.why3: I never had captions in my last conversation, so I am picturing glasses I have never worn and partly guessing whether my eyes could do both.
screens.why4: Yes easily, most of the time, only sometimes, and no are distinct and cover my true answers, and I can't tell fits when I've never tried it.
screens.why5: The card names the idea on purpose and the question uses plain words, not any founder jargon about users or segments.
screens.why6: Short single question, four short options I can hold, one escape said last; it sounds fine spoken.
screens.why7: An ability on the could-you-have measure with the ability four in order, two for and two against, the condition varies across deaf people, and I can't tell sits apart as the card requires.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the captions-while-watching-faces question, it makes sense to ask whether this would have helped me the last time I lost a conversation at a table.
screens.why2: "Have done that better" made me stop, because "that" points back to losing the conversation, and I don't want to lose it better; I want to follow it.
screens.why3: Losing the thread at a table full of hearing people talking over each other happens to me all the time, so I can picture the last one easily.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference and worse cover every answer I could give, and "I can't tell" fits if I'm unsure about glasses I've never worn.
screens.why5: The card says captions inside the lens of glasses, but the question shrinks it to "an app", and I already have captioning apps on my phone, so I might answer about the wrong thing.
screens.why6: Heard once, it is one question with four short options and one escape; the only awkward part is "done that better".
screens.why7: The four fixed answers and the escape are all there in order, so the belief can be supported or refuted, but "done that better" leaves unclear what would be better, which is the pitfall the card names.
screens.instead: Think of the most recent time you lost the conversation around a table with hearing people. Would AirCaps, captions inside your glasses, have helped you follow it, or not? A lot better · A little better · No difference · Worse · I can't tell

screens.why1: After asking whether captions would work and whether they'd beat what I do now, it makes sense to ask whether I'd actually put the glasses on and wear them when I'm talking with people.
screens.why2: Wearing glasses in a conversation is plain to me, and I'd answer it straight away.
screens.why3: I know how I feel about wearing something on my face while talking with hearing people, and how long a dinner or meeting runs, so I can answer from my own life.
screens.why4: Yes, a conditional yes, probably not, and no cover what I'd say, and comfort over a long conversation is a real catch for me, so it isn't just a second Yes.
screens.why5: The idea card names it on purpose, and the question only asks me to wear the glasses, with no plan or insider terms coming through.
screens.why6: It's one short question with four short options I can hold in my head and the escape said last, so I'd hear it once and answer.
screens.why7: Wearing the glasses is a step I take myself, all four options are on whether I'd take it, two count for and two against, the condition is specific to this step, and I can't tell sits apart as the card requires.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I'd wear the glasses, it makes sense to ask what would make the whole thing worth it to me before the study ends.
screens.why2: Short and plain; I'd get 'clearly worth it to you' the first time I read it or had it read to me, and it doesn't paste back any long wording of mine.
screens.why3: I know what I'd need from captions at a noisy table or a fast conversation, so I can answer from my own week.
screens.why4: It's a box to type in, with no options.
screens.why5: It only uses the AirCaps name already shown on the idea card, and nothing new from the founder's plan or their words for people leaks in.
screens.why6: One short question with no list, symbol or aside, easy to hear once and answer.
